grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('anoti')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'anoti' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('mavara')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'mavara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('matatu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'matatu' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Number Stem (-mwe = 1, -viri = 2, -tatu = 3, -na = 4, -shanu = 5) -> vanhu vaviri (2 people), maminitsi mashanu (5 minutes)

cultural_notes.title: National Symbols & Colours of Zimbabwe ('Mureza weZimbabwe')
cultural_notes.content: Every colour on the national flag of Zimbabwe ('mureza weZimbabwe') carries historical and natural meaning taught in schools across the country: green ('girinhi') represents the land's agriculture and vegetation, yellow ('yero') stands for mineral wealth, red ('tsvuku') honours the blood shed during the liberation struggle, black ('tema') represents the heritage of the majority people, and the white ('chena') triangle symbolizes peace.

options: 'Machena' means light grey while 'chena' means bright white
Only clothing can use the word 'chena'
'Machena' is only used in the past tense
Colour adjectives change their prefix to match the noun they describe ('ma-' for 'mabhuku')
active_exercises.correct_answer: Colour adjectives change their prefix to match the noun they describe ('ma-' for 'mabhuku')
active_exercises.explanation: In Shona, traditional colour stems (-chena, -tema, -tsvuku) take the prefix of the noun they describe.
